high.title: Exported receiver MyReceiver uses SEND_SMS for any app
high.description: MyReceiver is exported without a permission and uses an API guarded by android.permission.SEND_SMS, which the app holds, so any app that starts it gets that permission's effect without asking for it. The `MyReceiver` broadcast receiver is exported and lacks permission protection, allowing any application on the device to trigger the sending of SMS messages using the app's `SEND_SMS` permission.
high.impact: An attacker can send arbitrary SMS messages from the victim's device, potentially leading to financial loss or social engineering attacks.

lines_html: if (intent.getAction() != null && intent.getAction().equals("edu.ksu.cs.benign.myrecv")) {
java.lang.String number = intent.getStringExtra("number");
java.lang.String text = intent.getStringExtra("text");
android.telephony.SmsManager smsManager = android.telephony.SmsManager.getDefault();
smsManager.sendTextMessage(number, null, "Benign: " + text, null, null);
android.util.Log.d("Benign", "Message sent");

high.recommendation: Guard MyReceiver with a signature-level android:permission, or stop exporting it; and drop SEND_SMS if the app itself does not need it.

info.title: Missing screenshot protection
info.description: The app does not set `FLAG_SECURE` on its activities, meaning screen contents can be captured via screenshots or recordings.
info.impact: Sensitive information displayed on the screen may be leaked to other apps or the user's storage.
info.recommendation: Call `getWindow().setFlags(WindowManager.LayoutParams.FLAG_SECURE, WindowManager.LayoutParams.FLAG_SECURE)` in the `onCreate` method of sensitive activities.

reasons: Screen contents not protected from capture. Without FLAG_SECURE, what a screen shows can end up in screenshots, screen recordings and the task-switcher preview. That matters on screens showing credentials, card numbers or balances; on its own it is a hardening note.
Screen contents not protected from capture reaches at most CVSS 3.3 (Low); the vector given scores this finding above anything the class does.

info.title: No network security config declared
info.description: The app declares neither android:networkSecurityConfig nor usesCleartextTraffic, so it relies on platform defaults and pins no domain. With targetSdkVersion 27 those defaults still permit cleartext HTTP (see the cleartext finding).
info.impact: Without pinning, anyone who gets a CA trusted on the device can read and alter the app's TLS traffic.
info.recommendation: Declare a network security config that disables cleartext and pins the domains that carry sensitive traffic.

reasons: No certificate pinning. Pinning defends against an attacker who already controls a trusted CA or the device's trust store. Without one of those, TLS is still doing its job. It becomes a finding when paired with what the unpinned channel actually carries.
Lack of pinning is a step in a chain; TLS still provides baseline encryption.

info.title: targetSdkVersion 27 allows implicit component export
info.description: On targetSdk 27, any component with an intent-filter is exported unless it says otherwise.
info.recommendation: Raise targetSdkVersion to 31+ and declare android:exported explicitly on every filtered component.

reasons: Legacy platform behaviour from SDK levels. An SDK level is a statement about which platform defaults apply, not a defect. It is context for the findings that depend on those defaults - pair it with one of them.
Target SDK defaults permit implicit export, which is the entry point for The broadcast receiver 'MyReceiver' is exported and does not require.
warnings: Implicit export only applies below targetSdk 31; confirm the app's targetSdkVersion before treating this as exploitable.

info.title: targetSdkVersion 27 permits cleartext traffic by default
info.description: targetSdk 27 predates API 28, where cleartext HTTP became opt-in. The app targets API level 27, which allows cleartext HTTP traffic by default and permits implicit export of components with intent-filters.
info.impact: This increases the attack surface by potentially exposing the app to man-in-the-middle attacks and unintended component access.

reasons: Cleartext permitted by configuration. The flag permits HTTP; it does not show that anything is sent over it. Name a request that actually goes out in cleartext, and what it carries, and this is a genuine finding.
Target SDK defaults permit cleartext, but no specific HTTP request is demonstrated.
warnings: Cleartext is blocked by default from targetSdk 28; confirm the declared target and any network security config.

info.title: Task hijacking (StrandHogg) possible on Android 10 and lower
info.description: minSdkVersion 22 lets the app run on Android versions before 11, and its task affinity is its package name "edu.ksu.cs.benign". There, another app can declare the same affinity, with allowTaskReparenting, and have its own activity shown in this app's task. The app does not specify `android:taskAffinity=""` and targets a legacy SDK, making it potentially susceptible to task hijacking (StrandHogg) on older Android versions.
info.impact: A malicious app with the same task affinity could place its own activity on top of the target app's activity, tricking the user into providing credentials.
info.recommendation: Raise minSdkVersion to 30, where Android fixed this. Until then, android:taskAffinity="" on the <application> mitigates the original attack, though not its runtime variant on unpatched Android 9 and lower.
